beats.intro: Derivatives, module four. [[sub]]How derivative prices are pinned to spot prices: no arbitrage, replication, and the cost of carry.
beats.law: [[a]]An arbitrage is a riskless profit. The simplest case breaks the law of one price: identical assets trading at different prices. [[bonds]]Two identical zero-coupon bonds both pay one hundred euros at maturity. Bond A costs ninety-nine. Bond B costs ninety-nine fifteen. [[t0]]Today, sell bond B short for ninety-nine fifteen, and buy bond A for ninety-nine. You pocket fifteen cents. [[tt]]At maturity, bond A pays one hundred, which buys back bond B. Nothing is left to pay. [[end]]The profit is risk free. Buyers and sellers rush in, until the two prices are equal.
beats.known: [[a]]The second kind of arbitrage involves an asset with a known future price. Its spot price should equal the future price discounted at the risk-free rate. [[ex]]Gold is at seventeen seventy. Procam can sell it forward in three months at seventeen ninety-two thirteen. The risk-free rate is two percent. [[t0]]Today, Procam borrows to buy the gold, and agrees to sell it forward. The net cash flow is zero. [[tt]]In three months, it delivers the gold and receives seventeen ninety-two thirteen. It repays the loan: seventeen seventy-eight seventy-eight. [[pf]]The riskless profit is thirteen dollars thirty-five an ounce. [[fix]]Buying pushes the spot price up, until it reaches seventeen eighty-three twenty-eight, the discounted forward price, and the arbitrage disappears.
beats.price: [[a]]No arbitrage pins down the forward price. For an asset with no costs or benefits, the forward price equals the spot price, compounded at the risk-free rate for the life of the contract. [[r]]A higher rate, or a longer maturity, makes the forward price rise further above spot. [[neg]]If the risk-free rate were negative, the forward price would sit below spot.
beats.replicate: [[a]]Replication recreates a derivative from other positions. A long forward can be copied by borrowing the spot price today, buying the asset, and holding it to maturity. [[ex]]Gold is now seventeen eighty-three twenty-eight, and the forward price is seventeen ninety-two thirteen. [[hi]]If gold ends at nineteen hundred, the forward gains ten thousand seven hundred eighty-seven dollars on one hundred ounces. So does the borrow-and-buy strategy. [[lo]]If gold ends at seventeen hundred, both lose nine thousand two hundred thirteen. [[pt]]Same payoff in every outcome, so they must have the same price.
beats.riskfree: [[a]]Now combine a long position in the asset with a short forward. [[cf]]Procam pays one hundred seventy-eight thousand three hundred twenty-eight today, and receives one hundred seventy-nine thousand two hundred thirteen in three months, whatever gold does. [[r]]The return is exactly two percent: the risk-free rate. [[pt]]A hedged position earns the risk-free rate. That is what no arbitrage means.
beats.carry: [[a]]Owning the asset can cost money or pay money, and the forward price must reflect both. This net amount is the cost of carry. [[cost]]Costs raise the forward price: the risk-free rate, and storage and insurance for physical goods. [[ben]]Benefits lower it: dividends, coupons, and for commodities, a convenience yield. [[rule]]If costs exceed benefits, the forward is above spot. If benefits exceed costs, the forward is below spot. [[f]]With a known income or cost, the forward is spot, minus the present value of income, plus the present value of costs, all compounded at the risk-free rate.
beats.equity: [[a]]Take Unilever shares at fifty euros, a five percent rate, and six months. [[nod]]With no dividend, the forward price is fifty-one twenty-three. [[div]]Now add a thirty-cent dividend in three months, and another at maturity. Their present value is fifty-nine cents. [[calc]]Subtract it from spot, then compound: the forward falls to fifty euros sixty-three. [[idx]]For an index, income is a yield. A stock index at fifteen thousand two hundred, with a two point two percent yield and a four percent rate, has a three-month forward of fifteen thousand two hundred sixty-eight fifty-five.
beats.fx: [[a]]Currencies are a special case. Each currency has its own interest rate, and the forward rate depends on the difference between them. [[ex]]Take Australian dollars per US dollar, at one point three three three five. The Australian rate is lower, at zero point zero five percent, against zero point two zero percent in dollars. [[steps]]Borrow a thousand US dollars, convert them to one thousand three hundred thirty-three point fifty Australian dollars, and lend them. In six months you hold one thousand three hundred thirty-three eighty-three, and owe one thousand and one dollars. [[res]]The rate that exchanges one for the other, one point three three two five, is the forward rate. [[rule]]When the foreign rate is below the domestic rate, the forward is below spot. The forward depends on the interest rate gap, not on the level of rates.
beats.commodity: [[a]]For commodities, storage and insurance are real costs. [[ex]]Back to gold, at seventeen eighty-three twenty-eight, with a two percent rate. Add storage and insurance of two dollars an ounce, paid at the end. [[calc]]Its present value is a dollar ninety-nine. The forward becomes seventeen ninety-four thirteen, two dollars higher than before. [[cy]]If an actual forward price is well below this no-arbitrage level, the market may be pricing a convenience yield: a benefit of holding the physical commodity.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Arbitrage is a riskless profit, and no arbitrage pins derivative prices to spot prices. [[w2]]A forward is replicated by borrowing to buy the asset. [[w3]]The forward price is spot compounded at the risk-free rate. [[w4]]Costs of carry raise it, benefits such as dividends lower it, and currencies use the rate differential.
beats.finish: Module four complete. Next: pricing and valuing forward contracts.
